{{Short description|Geometry theorem}}
[[File:Pappus-proj-ev.svg|thumb|Pappus's hexagon theorem: Points ''X'', ''Y'' and ''Z'' are collinear on the Pappus line. The hexagon is ''AbCaBc''.]]
[[File:Pappus-aff-ev.svg|thumb|Pappus's theorem: affine form<br>
<math>Ab\parallel aB, Bc\parallel bC \Rightarrow Ac\parallel aC</math>]]

In [[mathematics]], '''Pappus's hexagon theorem''' (attributed to [[Pappus of Alexandria]]) states that 
if <math>A, B, C</math> is one set of [[Collinearity|collinear]] points, and <math>a,b,c</math> is another set of collinear points, then the intersection points <math>X,Y,Z</math> of [[line (mathematics)|line]] pairs <math>Ab</math> and <math>aB, Ac</math> and <math>aC, Bc</math> and <math>bC</math> are [[collinear]], lying on the ''Pappus line''. These three points are the points of intersection of the "opposite" sides of the hexagon <math>AbCaBc</math>. 

It holds in a [[projective plane]] over any field, but fails for projective planes over any noncommutative [[division ring]].<ref>Coxeter, pp. 236–7</ref> Projective planes in which the "theorem" is valid are called '''pappian planes'''.

If one considers a pappian plane containing a hexagon as just described but with sides <math>Ab</math> and <math>aB</math> [[Parallel (geometry)|parallel]] and also sides <math>Bc</math> and <math>bC</math> parallel (so that the Pappus line <math>u</math> is the [[line at infinity]]), one gets the [[Affine geometry#Pappus' law|''affine version'' of Pappus's theorem]] shown in the second diagram.

If the Pappus line <math>u</math> and the lines <math>g,h</math> have a point in common, one gets the so-called '''little''' version of Pappus's theorem.<ref> Rolf Lingenberg: ''Grundlagen der Geometrie'', BI-Taschenbuch, 1969, p. 93</ref>
 
The [[duality (projective geometry)|dual]] of this [[intersection theorem|incidence theorem]] states that given one set of [[concurrent lines]] <math>A, B, C</math>, and another set of concurrent lines <math>a, b, c</math>, then the lines <math>x, y, z</math> defined by pairs of points resulting from pairs of intersections <math>A\cap b</math> and <math>a\cap B, \; A\cap c</math> and <math>a\cap C, \;B\cap c</math> and <math>b\cap C</math> are concurrent. (''Concurrent'' means that the lines pass through one point.)

Pappus's theorem is a [[special case]] of [[Pascal's theorem]] for a conic—the [[limiting case (mathematics)|limiting case]] when the [[degenerate conic|conic degenerates]] into 2 straight lines. Pascal's theorem is in turn a special case of the [[Cayley–Bacharach theorem]].

The [[Pappus configuration]] is the [[projective configuration|configuration]] of 9 lines and 9 points that occurs in Pappus's theorem, with each line meeting 3 of the points and each point meeting 3 lines. In general, the Pappus line does not pass through the point of intersection of <math>ABC</math> and <math>abc</math>.<ref>However, this does occur when <math>ABC</math> and <math>abc</math> are in [[perspective (geometry)|perspective]], that is, <math>Aa, Bb</math> and <math>Cc</math> are concurrent.</ref>  This configuration is [[Duality (projective geometry)|self dual]]. Since, in particular, the lines <math>Bc, bC, XY</math> have the properties of the lines <math>x,y,z</math> of the dual theorem, and collinearity of <math>X,Y,Z</math> is equivalent to concurrence of <math>Bc, bC, XY</math>, the dual theorem is therefore just the same as the theorem itself. The [[Levi graph]] of the Pappus configuration is the [[Pappus graph]], a [[Bipartite graph|bipartite]] [[Distance-regular graph|distance-regular]] graph with 18 vertices and 27 edges.

== Proof: affine form ==
[[File:Pappus-proof-ev.svg|thumb|Pappus theorem: proof]]
If the affine form of the statement can be proven, then the projective form of Pappus's theorem is proven, as the extension of a pappian plane to a projective plane is unique. 

Because of the parallelity in an affine plane one has to distinct two cases: <math>g \not\parallel h</math> and <math>g \parallel h</math>. The key for a simple proof is the possibility for introducing a "suitable" [[coordinate system]]:

'''Case 1:''' The lines <math>g,h</math> intersect at point <math>S=g\cap h</math>.<br />
In this case coordinates are introduced, such that  <math>\;S=(0,0), \; A=(0,1), \;c=(1,0)\;</math> (see diagram). 
<math>B,C</math>  have the coordinates <math>\;B=(0,\gamma),\; C=(0,\delta), \; \gamma,\delta \notin \{0,1\}</math>.
 
From the parallelity of the lines <math>Bc,\; Cb</math> one gets <math>b=(\tfrac{\delta}{\gamma},0)</math> and the parallelity of the lines <math>Ab, Ba</math> yields <math>a=(\delta,0)</math>. Hence line <math>Ca</math> has slope <math>-1</math> and is parallel line <math>Ac</math>.

'''Case 2:''' <math>g\parallel h \ </math> (little theorem).<br />
In this case the coordinates are chosen such that <math>\;c=(0,0), \;b=(1,0),\; A=(0,1), \;B=(\gamma,1),\;\gamma\ne 0</math>. From the parallelity of <math>Ab\parallel Ba</math> and <math> cB\parallel bC</math> one gets <math>\;C=(\gamma+1,1)\;</math> and <math> \;a=(\gamma+1,0)\;</math>, respectively, and at least the parallelity <math>\;Ac\parallel Ca\;</math>.

== Proof with homogeneous coordinates ==
Choose [[homogeneous coordinates]] with 
:<math>C = (1, 0, 0), \; c= (0, 1, 0),\; X = (0, 0, 1), \; A = (1, 1, 1)</math>.
On the lines <math>AC, Ac, AX</math>, given by <math>x_2 = x_3,\; x_1 =x_3, \; x_2 = x_1</math>, take the points <math>B, Y, b</math> to be 
:<math>B = (p, 1, 1),\; Y = (1, q, 1),\; b = (1, 1, r)</math>
for some <math>p, q, r</math>. The three lines <math>XB, CY, cb</math> are <math>x_1 = x_2 p,\; x_2= x_3 q,\; x_3 = x_1 r</math>, so they pass through the same point <math>a</math> if and only if <math>rqp = 1</math>. The condition for the three lines <math>Cb, cB</math> and <math>XY</math> with equations <math> x_2 = x_1 q,\; x_1 = x_3 p ,\; x_3 = x_2 r</math> to pass through the same point <math>Z</math> is <math>rpq =1</math>. So this last set of three lines is concurrent if all the other eight sets are because multiplication is commutative, so <math>pq = qp</math>. Equivalently, <math>X, Y, Z</math> are collinear.

The proof above also shows that for Pappus's theorem to hold for a [[projective space]] over a division ring it is both sufficient and necessary that the division ring is a (commutative) field. German mathematician [[Gerhard Hessenberg]] proved that Pappus's theorem implies [[Desargues's theorem]].<ref name="Coxeter">{{harvnb|Coxeter|1969|loc=p. 238}}</ref><ref>According to {{harv|Dembowski|1968|loc= pg. 159, footnote 1}}, Hessenberg's original proof {{harvtxt|Hessenberg|1905}} is not complete; he disregarded the possibility that some additional incidences could occur in the Desargues configuration. A complete proof is provided by {{harvnb|Cronheim|1953}}.</ref> In general, Pappus's theorem holds for some projective plane [[if and only if]] it is a projective plane over a commutative field. The projective planes in which Pappus's theorem does not hold are [[Desarguesian]] projective planes over noncommutative division rings, and [[non-Desarguesian plane]]s.

The proof is invalid if <math>C, c, X</math> happen to be collinear. In that case an alternative proof can be provided, for example, using a different projective reference.

== Dual theorem ==
Because of the [[Duality (projective geometry)|principle of duality for projective planes]] the '''dual theorem of Pappus''' is true:

If 6 lines <math>A,b,C,a,B,c </math> are chosen alternately from two [[Pencil (mathematics)#Pencil of lines|pencils]] with centers <math>G,H</math>, the lines 
: <math> X:= (A\cap b) (a\cap B), </math>
: <math> Y:= (c\cap A) (C\cap a), </math>
: <math> Z:= (b\cap C) (B\cap c)</math>
are concurrent, that means: they have a point <math>U</math> in common.<br>
The left diagram shows the projective version, the right one an affine version, where the points 
<math>G,H</math> are points at infinity. If point <math>U</math> is on the line <math>GH</math> than one gets the "dual little theorem" of Pappus' theorem.
<gallery widths="250" heights="250" class="float-right">
Pappus-dual-proj-ev.svg|dual theorem: projective form
Pappus-dual-aff-ev.svg|dual theorem: affine form
</gallery>

If in the affine version of the dual "little theorem" point <math>U</math> is a [[point at infinity]] too, one gets [[Thomsen's theorem]], a statement on 6 points on the sides of a triangle (see diagram). The Thomsen figure plays an essential role coordinatising an axiomatic defined projective plane.<ref> W. Blaschke: ''Projektive Geometrie'', Springer-Verlag, 2013, {{ISBN|3034869320}}, S. 190</ref> The proof of the closure of Thomsen's figure is covered by the proof for the "little theorem", given above. But there exists a simple direct proof, too:

Because the statement of Thomsen's theorem (the closure of the figure) uses only the terms ''connect, intersect'' and ''parallel'', the statement is [[Affine map|affine]]ly invariant, and one can introduce coordinates such that 
<math>P=(0,0), \; Q=(1,0), \; R=(0,1)</math> (see right diagram). The starting point of the sequence of chords is <math>(0,\lambda).</math> One easily verifies the coordinates of the points given in the diagram, which shows: the last point coincides with the first point.
<gallery widths="250" heights="250" class="float-right">
Thomsen-kl-d-pap-ev.svg|''Thomsen figure'' (points <math>\color{red} 1,2,3,4,5,6 </math> of the triangle <math>PQR</math>) as dual theorem of the little theorem of Pappus (<math>U</math> is at infinity, too !).
Thomsen-beweis.svg|Thomsen figure: proof
</gallery>

==Other statements of the theorem==
[[Image:Pappus hexagon.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Triangles <math>XcC</math> and <math>BbY</math> are perspective from <math>A</math> and <math>a</math>, and so, also from <math>Z</math>.]]
In addition to the above characterizations of Pappus's theorem and its dual, the following are equivalent statements:
* If the six vertices of a hexagon lie alternately on two lines, then the three points of intersection of pairs of opposite sides are collinear.<ref>Coxeter, p. 231</ref>
* Arranged in a matrix of nine points (as in the figure and description above) and thought of as evaluating a [[Permanent (mathematics)|permanent]], if the first two rows and the six "diagonal" triads are collinear, then the third row is collinear.
::<math>\left|\begin{matrix}
A & B & C \\
a & b & c \\
X & Y & Z \end{matrix}
\right|</math>
:That is, if <math>\ ABC, abc, AbZ, BcX, CaY, XbC, YcA, ZaB\ </math> are lines, then Pappus's theorem states that <math>XYZ</math> must be a line.  Also, note that the same matrix formulation applies to the dual form of the theorem when <math>(A,B,C)</math> ''etc.'' are triples of concurrent lines.<ref name="Coxeter_a">Coxeter, p. 233</ref>
* Given three distinct points on each of two distinct lines, pair each point on one of the lines with one from the other line, then the joins of points not paired will meet in (opposite) pairs at points along a line.<ref>Whicher, chapter 14</ref>
* If two triangles are [[Perspective (geometry)|perspective]] in at least two different ways, then they are perspective in three ways.<ref name="Coxeter" />
* If <math>\; AB, CD,\;</math> and <math>EF</math> are concurrent and <math>DE, FA, </math> and <math>BC</math> are concurrent, then <math> AD, BE,</math>  and <math>CF</math> are concurrent.<ref name="Coxeter_a" />

==Origins==
What we call Pappus's Theorem is found in chapters 202, 206, 207, 209, and 211, also numbered as Propositions 134, 138, 139, 141, and 143, of Book VII of [[Pappus of Alexandria|Pappus's]] ''Collection''.<ref>Jones (p. 562) names these five propositions; Heath (Vol. II, p. 421) names only the last four.  The last two can be understood as converses of the second and third.  Kline (p. 128) cites only Proposition 139.  The numbering of the propositions is as assigned by Hultsch.</ref>  These are Lemmas VIII, XII, XIII, XV, and XVII in the part of Book VII consisting of lemmas to the first of the three books of [[Euclid]]'s ''Porisms.''
 
Lemma VIII is what is called above the affine version of Pappus's Theorem. Pappus proves it with areas.  In the figure below,
<math display=block>\varDelta E \ || \ B\varGamma \quad \& \quad EH\ || \ BZ.</math>
:[[File:Pappus-collection-7-ch-202-prop-134-hypothesis.svg|alt=The vertices of hexagon ''BΓHEΔZ'' lie alternately on ''BH'' and ''ΓZ'' and intersect at ''A'']]
We are going to show
<math display=block>\varDelta Z \ || \ \varGamma H.</math>
To do this, we draw {{mvar|BE}}, {{mvar|ΔΓ}}, and {{mvar|ZH}}.
:[[File:Pappus-collection-7-ch-202-prop-134.svg|alt=The vertices of hexagon ''BΓHEΔZ'' lie alternately on ''BH'' and ''ΓZ'' and intersect at ''A'', and lines ''BE'', ''ΔΓ'', and ''ZH'' are drawn]]
As triangles,
<math display=block>\triangle \varDelta BE = \triangle \varDelta \varGamma E.</math>
Adding {{math|△''ΔAE''}} to either side yields
<math display=block>\triangle ABE = \triangle \varDelta \varGamma A.</math>
Likewise,
<math display=block>\triangle BEZ = \triangle BHZ,</math>
and subtracting {{math|△''BAZ''}} yields
<math display=block>\triangle ABE = \triangle AHZ.</math>
From this and what we already know,
<math display=block>\triangle \varDelta \varGamma A = \triangle AHZ.</math>
Adding {{math|△''AΓH''}}, we obtain
<math display=block>\triangle \varDelta \varGamma H = \triangle Z\varGamma H,</math>
which gives us the parallelism that we want.

The other lemmas are proved in terms of what today is known as the cross ratio of four collinear points. Three earlier lemmas are used. The first of these, Lemma III, has the diagram below (which uses Pappus's lettering, with {{mvar|G}} for {{mvar|Γ}}, {{mvar|D}} for {{mvar|Δ}}, {{mvar|J}} for {{mvar|Θ}}, and {{mvar|L}} for {{mvar|Λ}}). 
:[[File:Pappus-collection-7-129.svg|Pappus-collection-7-129]]
Here three concurrent straight lines, {{mvar|AB}}, {{mvar|AG}}, and {{mvar|AD}}, are crossed by two lines, {{mvar|JB}} and {{mvar|JE}}, which concur at {{mvar|J}}. 
Also {{mvar|KL}} is drawn parallel to {{mvar|AZ}}.
Then
<math display=block>
  \overline{KJ} : \overline{JL} :: 
  \left( \overline{KJ} : \overline{AG} \ \& \ \overline{AG} : \overline{JL} \right) :: 
  \left(\overline{JD} : \overline{GD} \ \& \ \overline{BG} : \overline{JB} \right)
</math>
These proportions might be written today as equations:<ref>A reason for using the notation above is that, for the ancient Greeks, a ratio is not a number or a geometrical object.  We may think of ratio today as an equivalence class of pairs of geometrical objects. Also, equality for the Greeks is what we might today call congruence. In particular, distinct line segments may be equal.  Ratios are not ''equal'' in this sense; but they may be the ''same.''</ref>
<math display=block>
  \frac{\overline{KJ}}{\overline{JL}} 
  = \frac{\overline{KJ}}{\overline{AG}} \times \frac{\overline{AG}}{\overline{JL}} 
  = \frac{\overline{JD}}{\overline{GD}} \times \frac{\overline{BG}}{\overline{JB}}.</math>
The last compound ratio (namely {{math|''{{overline|JD}}'' : ''{{overline|GD}}'' & ''{{overline|BG}}'' : ''{{overline|JB}}''}}) is what is known today as the [[cross ratio]] of the collinear points {{mvar|J}}, {{mvar|G}}, {{mvar|D}}, and {{mvar|B}} in that order; it is denoted today by {{math|(''J'', ''G''; ''D'', ''B'')}}. So we have shown that this is independent of the choice of the particular straight line {{mvar|JD}} that crosses the three straight lines that concur at {{mvar|A}}. In particular
<math display=block>(J, G; D, B) = (J, Z; H, E).</math>
It does not matter on which side of {{mvar|A}} the straight line {{mvar|JE}} falls. In particular, the situation may be as in the next diagram, which is the diagram for Lemma X. 
:[[File:Pappus-collection-7-136.svg|Pappus-collection-7-136]]
Just as before, we have 
<math display=block>(J, G; D, B) = (J, Z; H, E).</math> 
Pappus does not explicitly prove this; but Lemma X is a converse, namely that if these two cross ratios are the same, and the straight lines {{mvar|BE}} and {{mvar|DH}} cross at {{mvar|A}}, then the points {{mvar|G}}, {{mvar|A}}, and {{mvar|Z}} must be collinear.

What we showed originally can be written as 
<math display=block>(J, \infty; K, L) = (J, G; D, B),</math>
with {{math|∞}} taking the place of the (nonexistent) intersection of {{mvar|JK}} and {{mvar|AG}}. Pappus shows this, in effect, in Lemma XI, whose diagram, however, has different lettering: 
:[[File:Pappus-collection-7-137.svg|Pappus-collection-7-137]]
What Pappus shows is 
<math display=block>\overline{DE} \cdot \overline{ZH} : \overline{EZ} \cdot \overline{HD} :: \overline{GB} : \overline{BE},</math> 
which we may write as
<math display=block>(D, Z; E, H) = (\infty, B; E, G).</math>
The diagram for Lemma XII is:
:[[File:Pappus-collection-7-138.svg|Pappus-collection-7-138]]
The diagram for Lemma XIII is the same, but {{mvar|{{overline|BA}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|DG}}}}, extended, meet at {{mvar|N}}. In any case, considering straight lines through {{mvar|G}} as cut by the three straight lines through {{mvar|A}}, (and accepting that equations of cross ratios remain valid after permutation of the entries,) we have by Lemma III or XI
<math display=block>(G, J; E, H) = (G, D; \infty Z).</math>
Considering straight lines through {{mvar|D}} as cut by the three straight lines through {{mvar|B}}, we have
<math display=block>(L, D; E, K) = (G, D; \infty Z).</math>
Thus 
<math display=block>(E, H; J, G) = (E, K; D, L),</math>
so by Lemma X, the points {{mvar|H}}, {{mvar|M}}, and {{mvar|K}} are collinear.  That is, the points of intersection of the pairs of opposite sides of the hexagon {{mvar|ADEGBZ}} are collinear.

Lemmas XV and XVII are that, if the point {{mvar|M}} is determined as the intersection of {{mvar|HK}} and {{mvar|BG}}, then the points {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|M}}, and {{mvar|D}} are collinear.  That is, the points of intersection of the pairs of opposite sides of the hexagon {{mvar|BEKHZG}} are collinear.
